article.overview: A precision timing instrument is a clock-based payload that provides a stable, traceable time reference for navigation, communication and geodesy on the Moon. Its core element is an atomic or ultra-stable oscillator, supported by electronics that timestamp signals and exchange time information with other clocks, spacecraft or ground stations. On Earth, GPS and Galileo depend on precise clocks in orbit. A lunar equivalent would need its own time reference, because the Moon's gravity and orbital motion cause its clocks to run at a different rate from clocks on Earth. The sources reviewed describe the concept mainly as simulations, prototypes and proposals. No flown precision timing instrument for the Moon was identified.
article.description: Lunar precision timing is needed because navigation depends on time. A receiver determines its position by measuring signal travel times from several transmitters, so clock errors propagate directly into position errors. A timing error of a few hundred nanoseconds corresponds to a trajectory error of kilometres, according to an Open Lunar blog post (a secondary source). A precision timing instrument would typically contain a frequency reference (a chip-scale atomic clock, a rubidium atomic frequency standard or an ultra-stable oscillator); electronics that produce a pulse-per-second or equivalent output; a communications or ranging interface for synchronising with other clocks, ground stations or spacecraft; and, in some designs, a receiver that uses signals from other navigation systems to correct the clock and orbit. The NASA LCRNS PNT Instrument (Example 1) follows this pattern with a weak-signal GNSS receiver, a navigation processor and a clock subsystem. The ESA-linked ATLAS study (Example 2) models spacecraft that exchange time signals with each other and with ground stations.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The purpose of a precision timing instrument is to maintain a stable, accurate time scale that can support autonomous navigation, navigation services for surface and orbital users, communication and networking, geodesy and reference frames, and relativistic and scientific studies. For autonomous navigation, a spacecraft in lunar orbit such as a relay can estimate its position, velocity and time onboard, reducing reliance on ground tracking; the NASA Goddard study addresses this for a relay (Ashman et al., 2024). A lunar positioning system would need a common reference clock or clock network; ESA's ATLAS study models a four-satellite constellation for this purpose (Sesta et al., 2025). Time synchronisation is also needed to coordinate communications between spacecraft and ground stations. Precise time is linked to the definition of a lunar reference frame and the lunar geodetic system; NASA's LCRNS documentation lists a defined lunar geodetic system and lunar time as dependencies for PNT services (NASA LCRNS presentation, 2025). The NIST work on a lunar coordinate time framework is a theoretical study of how lunar clocks would be defined and compared with Earth time (Ashby and Patla, 2024).
article.operating_principle: A precision timing instrument keeps time by counting oscillations of a stable frequency source. Atomic clocks use a transition in atoms, such as rubidium or caesium, as their reference; a chip-scale atomic clock is a miniaturised version of this approach; an ultra-stable oscillator uses a precisely controlled electronic resonator. Each has different stability over short and long periods, and performance depends strongly on clock quality. For navigation, time is used through measurements. Pseudorange measurements compare the signal delay from a transmitter, with the clock error estimated together with position. Doppler measurements, which reflect changes in signal frequency due to motion, are used to estimate velocity and orbit. Two-way time transfer allows two clocks to exchange signals in both directions and synchronise while correcting for travel time. The ATLAS study describes an asynchronous two-way method estimated at below 1 ns (about 0.3 ns with periodic calibration) and a coherent two-way ranging method that it estimates could reach about the 1 ns level (Sesta et al., 2025). A relativistic effect must also be handled: NIST reports that atomic clocks on the lunar surface would tick faster than clocks on Earth by about 56 microseconds per day, mainly because of the Moon's weaker gravity (NIST, 2024). A lunar time system must therefore include a defined correction and a reference scale. The Ashby and Patla framework is one proposal for this; the ATLAS study notes that the time scale for a navigation system remains open (Sesta et al., 2025).
article.scientific_importance: Precise timing underpins almost every other lunar navigation and communication function. Without a common time reference, separate spacecraft, landers and ground stations cannot exchange navigation signals reliably. The field is recent. The NIST framework (2024), the NASA Goddard relay study (2024) and the ESA-linked ATLAS study (2025) are among the most relevant sources identified. Their importance lies in the design questions they raise: whether lunar time should be set independently on the Moon or kept synchronised with Earth; how clocks should be distributed between surface and orbit; and how much clock quality is needed for a given navigation accuracy. The Ashman et al. (2024) study reports that clock quality is the strongest determinant of achievable performance in its simulations.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for a precision timing instrument. Mass, size, power and performance depend on clock technology, navigation architecture and mission. The examples are not directly comparable: Example 1 is a simulated relay payload, Example 2 is a constellation-level model and Example 3 is a laboratory prototype. Values are given only where the source states them.

examples.name: NASA Goddard LCRNS PNT Instrument (LPI)
examples.type: Simulated relay navigation payload concept (under development)
examples.status: Simulation results, compared with hardware-in-the-loop and software-in-the-loop lab tests. No flight demonstration described.
examples.components: NavCube3-mini weak-signal multi-frequency GNSS receiver, Goddard autonomous navigation software and a clock subsystem.
examples.notes: Mass, power and size are not stated in the conference paper reviewed. The CSAC is described as radiation-tolerant with low SWaP; the USO is the higher-performance alternative. The paper covers only part of the solution for relay PNT service.

examples.name: ESA ATLAS study lunar navigation constellation (modelled on ESA Moonlight)
examples.type: Modelled lunar radio navigation constellation (simulation study)
examples.status: Simulation only, using ESA GODOT orbit determination software and a Monte Carlo analysis of 577 arcs. No flight demonstration reported.
examples.constellation: Four small satellites in elliptical lunar frozen orbits (ELFOs) on two orbital planes, with aposelene over the southern hemisphere.
examples.mass_note: The study assumes about 230 kg per spacecraft, described as a SmallSat-class assumption because no consolidated design exists. This is not a verified spacecraft mass.
examples.rf_system_power_note: Estimated power for the radio-frequency system, including transponder and clock.
examples.ground_stations: Three ESTRACK sites (Cebreros, New Norcia, Malargüe); maximum visibility gap about 6 hours at 15° minimum elevation.
examples.clock_notes: The miniRAFS is the baseline for the headline results. The USO has the best short-term stability but the worst long-term stability.

performance.signal_in_space_error_m: up to 20 after 10 hours (95th percentile) or 6 hours (99th percentile), simulation
performance.requirement_statement: The conclusion states that a 20 m SISE requirement is met up to 10 hours in 95% of cases.
performance.orbit_accuracy: from a few centimetres to 10 m, simulation

examples.name: University of Neuchâtel miniature rubidium clock
examples.status: Prototype; must be qualified for space missions. No qualification schedule, named lunar mission or performance specification identified.
examples.clock_type: Ultra-miniaturised rubidium atomic clock read out with lasers
examples.heritage_notes: ESA has supported the university's miniaturisation work (AMICC project). Temex Neuchâtel Time, a related company, has earlier experience with space rubidium clocks; that experience is not specific to this prototype.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: No universal dimensions exist for a precision timing instrument. Dimensions of the NASA LPI and the Neuchâtel clock were not stated in the sources reviewed. The ATLAS study assumes a SmallSat-class spacecraft. Size depends on clock technology: a chip-scale atomic clock, a rubidium standard and an ultra-stable oscillator differ substantially in volume.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: Only the ATLAS study gives a mass figure, and it is an assumed value of about 230 kg per spacecraft for a SmallSat-class design. No verified mass is published for the NASA LPI or the Neuchâtel clock in the sources reviewed.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: The ATLAS study estimates about 90 W for the radio-frequency system, including transponder and clock, and about 515 W from a 1.5 m² solar array at 25% efficiency. No power figure is published for the NASA LPI or the Neuchâtel clock in the sources reviewed.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: A lunar timing instrument must operate in vacuum, with large temperature swings, radiation and micrometeoroid exposure. Atomic clocks are sensitive to temperature, vibration and magnetic fields, so their thermal and mechanical environment directly affects timing performance. The NASA LCRNS study describes the chip-scale atomic clock as radiation-tolerant. For a surface clock, the instrument would need stable mounting, thermal control and reliable power and data interfaces. For an orbiting clock, it would need coordination with attitude, communication and thermal systems. Timing performance also depends on a defined time scale and on accurate orbit and clock models. The ATLAS study reports synchronisation to Earth station clocks at about the 1 ns level, and the NIST work shows that relativistic corrections must be part of the time system.
article.limitations: Clock quality determines performance; the NASA study reports that clock stability is the strongest determinant of performance in its simulations. Both the LPI and ATLAS results are simulations, with lab tests in one case; neither is a flight result. Lunar clocks run faster than Earth clocks by about 56 microseconds per day (NIST, 2024), so any lunar time system must model this effect and be agreed between users. Choices of lunar time scale and reference frame remain under discussion between agencies and standards bodies (Sesta et al., 2025). The NASA study covers only part of the solution for a relay PNT service; a relay provider must also account for on-board delays, antenna displacements and other error sources (Ashman et al., 2024). The Open Lunar post suggests that clocks in a $50–5000 range may be suitable for some missions; this is a secondary claim and not a validated requirement.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: A precision timing instrument could be delivered as a fixed surface clock at a landing site or as part of an orbiting relay or navigation satellite. No specific lander, relay or spacecraft has been identified as compatible with a particular timing instrument in the sources reviewed.
transportation_process: Integrate the instrument with the lander or spacecraft on Earth.
Launch it using a launch vehicle.
Transfer it towards the Moon, either as a lunar surface delivery or as a lunar orbit insertion.
For a surface clock: deliver it by lander to the surface, deploy it at a surveyed location with stable mounting, thermal protection and power and data connections.

For an orbiter or relay: commission the clock and synchronise it with the spacecraft's navigation and communications systems, then establish orbit determination, antenna pointing and thermal interfaces.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: A surface clock would be placed by a lander or astronaut at a chosen location and surveyed, because its position would contribute to the lunar geodetic reference. An orbiting clock would be commissioned as part of the spacecraft after orbit insertion. The method depends on the mission architecture and is not specified in the sources reviewed.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: No flown lunar precision timing instrument was identified in the sources reviewed. The NASA LCRNS presentation describes NASA's intent to deliver LunaNet-compliant PNT services through commercial relay providers; this does not establish compatibility for any named instrument.
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: Compatibility with a specific lander, relay or spacecraft has not been verified. It would need to be assessed against verified interface documents covering mass, dimensions, mounting, power, data, thermal and timing-reference interfaces. The NASA LCRNS presentation was not read in full, so its interface requirements are not confirmed here.

article.historical_significance: No flown lunar precision timing instrument was identified in the sources reviewed. Historical significance therefore lies mainly in the recent development of lunar time and navigation concepts: the NIST lunar coordinate time framework (2024), the NASA Goddard LCRNS PNT Instrument study (2024), the ESA-linked ATLAS constellation study (2025) and the University of Neuchâtel miniature clock prototype. Together, they show that lunar time has become a practical engineering requirement as more missions and relays are planned.
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: Most of the material is simulation, proposal or prototype, and no flown example was identified. Only the ATLAS study gives mass and power figures, and its 230 kg spacecraft mass is an assumption. The LPI conference paper gives no mass, power or size. No stability figures were identified for the Neuchâtel prototype or the LPI clock. Several sources were reviewed through summaries and press coverage rather than the primary document: the NASA LCRNS presentation, the Neuchâtel clock coverage and the NIST paper (cited via the NIST release). Figures attributed to ATLAS were taken from a structured reading of the paper and should be checked against the full text. The lunar time standard is not settled.
